country.title: Bolivia
country.text:
Bolivia, officially the Plurinational State of Bolivia, is a landlocked country located in central South America. Its geography primarily consists of an Andean region to the west and tropical lowlands to the east and north. The country has a diverse environment, including the vast Amazonian plain, the Gran Chaco, temperate valleys, the high-altitude Altiplano plateau, snow-capped peaks, and mountains, encompassing a wide range of climates and biomes across its regions and cities. It includes part of the Pantanal, the largest tropical wetland in the world, along its eastern border. Bolivia is bordered by Brazil to the north and east, Paraguay to the southeast, Argentina to the south, Chile to the southwest, and Peru to the west. The seat of government is La Paz, which contains the executive, legislative, and electoral branches of government, while the constitutional capital is Sucre, the seat of the judiciary. While most population and urban centers lie in the Andean region, the largest city and principal industrial center is Santa Cruz de la Sierra, located in the eastern tropical lowlands.
Bolivia is a constitutionally unitary state divided into nine departments. Its geographic Andean-lowland divide is matched by economic and cultural differences such as those associated with the camba and colla demonyms. One-third of the country is within the Andean mountain range. With an area of 1,098,581 square kilometers (424,164 sq mi), Bolivia is the fifth-largest country in South America and, alongside Paraguay, is one of two landlocked countries in the Americas. It is the largest landlocked country in the Southern Hemisphere; it has inland ports accessing the Atlantic Ocean through two river systems: Acre-Purus-Amazon and Paraguay-Paraná. Bolivia had a population of 11.4 million as of the latest census in 2024. It is multiethnic, including Amerindians, Mestizos, and the descendants of Europeans and Africans. Spanish is the official and predominant language, although 36 indigenous languages also have official status, of which the most commonly spoken are Guaraní, Aymara, and Quechua.
Centuries prior to Spanish colonization, the region formed part of the Tiwanaku polity, which collapsed around 1000 AD. The Colla–Inca War of the 1440s marked the beginning of Inca rule in western Bolivia. The eastern and northern lowlands were inhabited by independent non-Andean Amazonian and Guaraní tribes. Spanish conquistadores arriving from Cusco, Peru and Asunción, Paraguay, forcibly took control of the region in the 16th century.
During the subsequent Spanish colonial period, Bolivia was administered by the Real Audiencia of Charcas. Spain built a large part of its global empire upon the massive silver reserves from Cerro Rico in Potosí. Following an unsuccessful rebellion in Sucre on May 25, 1809, sixteen years of fighting would follow before the establishment of the republic, named for Simón Bolívar. Over the course of the 19th and early 20th centuries, Bolivia lost control of several peripheral territories to neighboring countries, such as the Acre territory after Brazil's 1899–1903 takeover, and the Pacific coastal region which Chile seized in 1879.
Bolivia was ruled by an oligarchy composed of land-owning and mining interests, in which the people who were apart of the oligarchy were Simón Iturri Patiño, Moritz Hochschild, and Carlos Víctor Aramayo, until the Bolivian National Revolution of 1952 established universal suffrage, nationalized lucrative tin mining and made a limited land reform. There was a succession of military and civilian governments with the last non-elected military ruler leaving office in 1982.
Modern Bolivia is a member of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM), Organization of American States (OAS), Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization (ACTO), Bank of the South, the Union of South American Nations (USAN), and Southern Common Market (Mercosur). Bolivia remains a developing country, the second-poorest in South America, though it has slashed poverty rates. Its main economic resources include agriculture, forestry, fishing, mining, and goods such as textiles and clothing, refined metals, and refined petroleum. Bolivia is very geologically rich, with mines producing tin, lithium, silver, and copper. It is known for its production of coca plants and refined cocaine. In 2021, estimated coca cultivation and cocaine production was reported to be 39,700 hectares and 317 metric tons, respectively.

relations.title: Bolivia–China relations
relations.text:
The Plurinational State of Bolivia and the People's Republic of China officially established bilateral relations on July 9, 1985.


== History ==
Since the establishment of diplomatic ties between China and Bolivia in 1985, relations have expanded from economic and cultural ties to military, transport, infrastructure, raw materials, education and other areas.
The two countries celebrated 25th anniversary of diplomatic ties in Beijing, July 9, 2010.
In August 2010, China and Bolivia agreed to continue to develop military ties and cooperation. Relations between the two countries have deteriorated since their peak under the governments of Evo Morales and Luis Arce.


== Bilateral relations ==
Bilateral trade between Bolivia and China began at approximately $4 million, and has increased to over $27.76 million in 2002.
China's exports to Bolivia includes hardware, machinery, light industrial goods, textiles and daily necessities.
Bolivian exports to China were lumber and mineral ore.
China provided support for the establishment of the Bolivian Space Agency and the launch of its first satellite in 2014 for a total cost of US$300 million. China and also provides loans, e.g. of 67 million dollars to upgrade infrastructure in the Oruro region.
A Chinese firm is a partner in a lithium mining operation in Bolivia valued at $2.3 billion.
Bolivia joined the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) in 2018.
In July 2019, UN ambassadors of 37 countries, including Bolivia, signed a joint letter to the United Nations Human Rights Council defending China's persecution of Uyghurs in Xinjiang. Bolivia was one of 16 countries that defended China's policies in Xinjiang in 2019 but did not do so in 2020.
In June 2023, Bolivia turned to China for assistance amid the former's first economic crisis since the early 2000s.
In February 2024, Bolivia obtained a $350 million loan from China to build a zinc refining factory.


== Surveillance systems ==
In 2019, China developed the purpose of overhauling the Bolivian security system worth more than 105 million dollars. This system comprises new surveillance cameras, drones, automated evidence processing systems, and increased manpower to manage each of these new technologies, which have been collectively dubbed the BOL 110. The Bolivian Government said BOL 110 implementing artificial intelligence to counter crime. Some individuals have expressed concern about the nature and the pervasiveness of these technologies, however, and how they may be used to create a Bolivian police state. The recent employment of dubious surveillance and manipulation tactics by the Bolivian government may validate these concerns, with some scholars going so far as to warn that similar systems can encourage authoritarian practices.

worldbank.title: Bolivia - First Fiscal Sustainability and Economic Growth Development Policy Financing : Chair Summary
worldbank.project: BO-Bolivia First Fiscal Sustainability and Economic Growth Development Policy Financing -- P518208
worldbank.abstract: Executive Directors approved an IBRD Development Policy Financing for the Plurinational State of Bolivia, recognizing progress under the economic stabilization program and ongoing adjustments to restore fiscal and debt sustainability, including reducing the fiscal deficit, ending monetary financing, moving to a market exchange rate, and aligning domestic fuel prices with international parity, while leveraging the upcoming Country Partnership Framework (CPF) to strengthen institutions for private sector-led growth and more and better jobs. Directors noted the high risk of the operation and emphasized robust social protection through measures such as cash transfers under the Extraordinary Equity and Protection Program, improvements to the social registry, and a social spending floor under the IMF program, and called for close coordination with the IMF and other development partners and mobilization of World Bank Group (WBG), International Finance Corporation (IFC), and Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA) expertise to sustain reforms that stabilize the economy, strengthen fiscal sustainability, and advance inclusive growth.

worldbank.title: Bolivia - First Fiscal Sustainability and Economic Growth Development Policy Financing Project
worldbank.project: BO-Bolivia First Fiscal Sustainability and Economic Growth Development Policy Financing -- P518208
worldbank.abstract: The development objective of the Bolivia First Fiscal Sustainability and Economic Growth Development Policy Financing for Bolivia is to support the Government of Bolivia to implement key policy reforms aimed to strengthen fiscal sustainability and to promote private sector development. The operation focuses on two areas of work. First, it supports strengthening fiscal sustainability while protecting the poor and vulnerable by: establishing an extraordinary cash transfer mechanism as a bridge to an adaptive social protection system and a future Social Registry; modernizing public spending through restrictions on non-competitive procurement; introducing an exceptional, time-bound regime to reorganize, dissolve, or liquidate non-viable state-owned enterprises; and creating a fiscally sustainable fuel market by authorizing private fuel imports, liberalizing private retail fuel prices, and adopting an automatic diesel pricing mechanism linked to international benchmarks. worldbank.title: Macro Poverty Outlook for Bolivia : Annual Meetings 2026
worldbank.abstract: Output is contracting under fiscal and external imbalances accumulated for over a decade. The government has launched a stabilization effort, including fuel subsidy reform and exchange rate unification, anchored by an International Monetary Fund (IMF) program under preparation, though these will weigh on economic activity in the near term. Sustaining fiscal consolidation, protecting vulnerable households, and unlocking private investment are essential to restore growth and reduce poverty

worldbank.title: Bolivia - Santa Cruz Road Corridor Connector Project (San Ignacio-San José) : Recommendation for Verification of the Implementation of the Management Action Plan in Response to the Inspection Panel Investigation
worldbank.project: BO-Santa Cruz Road Corridor Connector Project (San Ignacio - San Jose) -- P152281
worldbank.abstract: On December 19, 2022, the Inspection Panel received a Request for Inspection related to the World Bank financed Bolivia: Santa Cruz Road Corridor Connector Project (San Ignacio-San José). The Panel investigated Bank Management’s compliance with its policies on Environmental Assessment, Indigenous Peoples, and Involuntary Resettlement as well as the Bank Policy on Investment Project Financing and the associated Directive. On February 12, 2024, the Panel submitted its Investigation Report to the Bank’s Board of Executive Directors. In its Investigation Report from February 2024, the Panel made several findings of non-compliance and concluded that these adversely affected marginalized communities, particularly the 17 Indigenous Chiquitano communities who live across four municipalities within the Project area.

worldbank.title: Bolivia - Santa Cruz Road Corridor Connector Project : Second Progress Report on the Implementation of the Management Action Plan in response to the Inspection Panel Investigation Report
worldbank.project: BO-Santa Cruz Road Corridor Connector Project (San Ignacio - San Jose) -- P152281
worldbank.abstract: This is the second Progress Report to the Board of Executive Directors (the “Board”) on the implementation of the Management Action Plan (MAP) in response to the Inspection Panel Investigation Report No. 187506-BO, dated February 12, 2024, on the Plurinational State of Bolivia: Santa Cruz Road Corridor Connector Project (P152281, the Project). The Project is a 230 million dollar operation 200 million dollar IBRD loan 30 million dollar IDA credit approved on January 11, 2017, with an original closing date of December 31, 2021. The Project Development Objective (PDO) is to improve transport accessibility along the road corridor between San Ignacio de Velasco and San José de Chiquitos by upgrading the approximately 208-kilometer road connecting these two municipal capitals in the department of Santa Cruz. This includes the construction of bypasses in populated areas, three small bridges, and approximately 300 culverts. The implementation agency is the Bolivian Highway Administration, Administradora Boliviana de Carreteras (ABC). The Project was expected to benefit 125,000 inhabitants, of whom 51 percent are considered poor and 62 percent are of indigenous descent.
